metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you ask Claude to improve your CLAUDE.md file, does it rewrite the file right away — or does something else have to happen first? Lands the carry-out that Claude scores the file against a fixed rubric before it changes anything, and every change after that is a diff with a reason, never a silent rewrite.

beats.narration_text: People assume asking Claude to improve a CLAUDE.md means it rewrites the file on the spot. Here's what's actually happening — it scores first, against a fixed rubric, before touching a single line. So: will it just score my CLAUDE.md?

beats.narration_text: Here's how discovery works. CLAUDE.md files live in five spots — the project root, shared with the team and checked into git; a local override, gitignored for personal settings; a global file, for your defaults across every project; a package-specific file inside each folder of a monorepo; and any subdirectory, for feature-scoped context. Claude walks parent directories to find them all. Then each file gets scored against six criteria — commands and workflows documented, architecture clarity, non-obvious patterns, conciseness, currency, and actionability — and comes back as a letter grade, A through F. They optimized for measurement before mutation: nothing changes until you've seen the grade.

The process runs in three phases. First, discovery — every CLAUDE.md gets found. Second, scoring — each one goes through the rubric. Third — and this is a hard rule wired into the skill — the full report shows up before a single line changes. Only after you say go does it propose updates, and every update arrives as a diff: which file, exactly what to add, and one line on why it helps future sessions. They optimized for consent over speed: minimal, targeted additions, never a wholesale rewrite of what's already there.

beats.narration_text: One trade-off worth naming. The discovery step caps at fifty files. In a small project that limit is invisible. In a large monorepo with more than fifty CLAUDE.md files, the ones past the cutoff never get read — silently, with no line in the report telling you they were skipped. This works if you value a bounded, predictable pass; it fails if you need proof the audit was complete.
Claude scores your CLAUDE.md against a fixed rubric before it touches a single line, and every change after that arrives as a diff with a reason — never a silent rewrite.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to write or audit a CLAUDE.md for my codebase. Ask me five questions — the stack and a one-sentence purpose, two or three commands I run every day, one non-obvious pattern a new contributor would trip over, which parts of the codebase are stable versus in-flux, and what's already documented elsewhere that I shouldn't repeat. Then draft a CLAUDE.md under two hundred lines from my answers, grade it A through F on the same six criteria — commands documented, architecture clarity, non-obvious patterns named, conciseness, currency, actionability — and show me only the sections scoring below A, each with a one-line reason. Go deeper: paste your existing CLAUDE.md back in, ask the same model for the same six-criteria grade, and have it show only the diff it would propose — each edit with one line on why it helps a future session.
